overview.title: Venom, decade by decade
overview.lede: Venom is the only major Marvel character who started as a costume. The black suit was a design problem — Jim Shooter wanted a new look for Spider-Man to sell Secret Wars — and the concept was bought from a reader, Randy Schueller, for $220. Everything since is people finding out what was inside it: first a costume that turns out to be alive, then a stalker with a grudge, then a 1990s anti-hero who outsold the book he came from, then a soldier, then a god. No other character on this site changes species this often, and the shelf is a record of an idea being repeatedly re-explained by whoever had it next.

sections.h: A costume, and then a man inside it
body: Spider-Man comes home from Secret Wars in a black suit in May 1984, and for four years the story is entirely about the suit. Mike Zeck drew the final design; the white spider stretched across the whole chest, no webbing lines, no red — and it is a genuinely great piece of costume design, which is the reason any of this happened.

Amazing Spider-Man #258 is where Reed Richards tells Peter it is alive, and #300 — May 1988, the anniversary issue — is where it finds somebody who wants it. David Michelinie invents Eddie Brock, a disgraced journalist who blames Spider-Man for his career, and puts him in a church with a costume that blames Spider-Man for everything else.

Todd McFarlane draws it, and the drawing is the character. The printed suit was a neat, tight bodysuit; McFarlane draws it as something that does not fit — too much of it, hanging in folds, with a mouth that is wider than the head it is on and a tongue nobody asked for. Marvel's own model sheets spent years catching up to what he did on the page.
What makes it work as horror is scale. Venom is drawn bigger than Spider-Man in every panel of #300, and he knows where Peter lives, which no other villain did.

fig.cap: Left: Amazing Spider-Man #252, May 1984 — the suit comes home and nobody knows it is alive. Right: #300, May 1988, McFarlane's first full Venom.

makers.b: Look at the slack. Every earlier artist drew the black suit skin-tight; McFarlane gives it too much material, so it pools at the wrists and pulls in long diagonal creases across the chest. That one decision is what turns a costume into something wearing a person.

Watch what he refuses to do: Venom never fights Spider-Man first. He turns up in Peter's flat, talks to Mary Jane, waits on the ceiling. The threat is domestic before it is physical, which is why the character landed.

sections.h: The lethal protector, and eighteen miniseries
body: Venom outsells the book he is a villain in, so in 1993 Marvel gives him his own — and immediately has to make him someone you can root for. Lethal Protector moves Eddie to San Francisco, gives him a colony of homeless people living under the city to defend, and has him agree not to eat anyone Spider-Man would mind about. It is a hairpin turn and it worked: the first issue, with a holographic foil cover, is one of the best-selling comics of the speculation boom.

Then comes the strangest publishing decision on this shelf. Marvel does not give him an ongoing. Instead, for five years, he gets a rolling sequence of three-issue miniseries — roughly eighteen of them — each with its own #1 to sell. Funeral Pyre, The Madness, Nights of Vengeance, Separation Anxiety, Carnage Unleashed, The Hunger, On Trial, License to Kill.
The strategy tells you exactly what Marvel thought it had: not a character, a brand with a number one on it. It also burned the character out, which is why he vanishes almost entirely after 1998.

There is real work in there. Sinner Takes All puts the symbiote on Eddie's ex-wife Anne Weying and is the only book of the era with an emotional idea in it; The Hunger establishes that the suit needs a brain chemical Eddie cannot supply and has him eating chocolate in an alley, which is both silly and the best horror beat of the decade; On Trial has Matt Murdock defending Eddie Brock in open court.

fig.cap: Left: Lethal Protector #1, 1993 — foil cover, a million copies, and the moment he becomes a hero. Right: Sinner Takes All, where the suit goes to Anne Weying.

makers.b: Lim draws Venom clean, and it is worth seeing what that costs. His figures are legible, well-staged and completely un-frightening; the same character that was a horror image under McFarlane reads here as a muscular action lead. That shift, more than any script, is what turns Venom into a hero.

sections.h: Carnage, and the problem with a sequel
body: Cletus Kasady arrives in 1992 out of the obvious idea: if the symbiote can bond to a man with a grudge, what happens if it bonds to a man with nothing else. Mark Bagley designs him as Venom without the mass — thin, red, all tendril and no bulk — which is the right call, because it makes him read as faster rather than stronger.

Maximum Carnage in 1993 is fourteen parts across four Spider-Man titles and is the high-water mark of the era's excess. It is also the story that forces Venom into the hero seat permanently: the only way to make Carnage frightening is to have Venom be the one frightened of him.

That is the structural problem the character never solves. Every escalation needs a worse thing above it, and each one pushes Venom further down the bill — which is how you end up, twenty-five years later, with a god.
sections.shelfLabel: Both ends of the Carnage story

sections.h: The ongoing at last, and then Eddie sells the suit
body: The character disappears for a year, comes back as a Spider-Man villain, and in 2003 finally gets the ongoing he was denied in 1993. Daniel Way and Francisco Herrera's Venom is eighteen issues about a symbiote thawed out of Antarctic ice, and it is a much odder book than its reputation — more body horror than action, with long stretches where nobody understands what is happening, deliberately.

Venom Vs. Carnage (2004) does the escalation trick one more time and produces Toxin, Carnage's offspring, bonded to a New York police officer. Clayton Crain paints it digitally, and it is the first time the symbiotes are rendered as wet rather than drawn as costume.

Then the run ends with something no other character on this site does. Eddie Brock, dying of cancer, auctions the symbiote off — and Mac Gargan, the Scorpion, buys it. The Venom that goes on to join the Thunderbolts and the Dark Avengers is not Eddie at all, and Eddie's story is over for the better part of a decade.

fig.cap: Left: Venom (2003) #1 — the first ongoing, ten years after the first miniseries. Right: Venom Vs. Carnage, painted by Clayton Crain.

sections.h: Flash Thompson, and the best premise the character ever had
body: Rick Remender takes the piece nobody had used — the symbiote is an addiction — and builds a whole book on it. Flash Thompson, Peter Parker's high-school bully turned Army sergeant, has lost both legs in Iraq. The government offers him the symbiote for fifty missions, and the suit gives him his legs back for the length of the mission and no longer.

Flash is the son of an alcoholic and is a drinker himself, and the book never once has to say so out loud: the thing that makes him whole is on a hard clock and he will do anything for one more hour of it. It is the cleanest metaphor any Venom comic has had.

Tony Moore draws the launch, and the design is the other good decision — a black tactical suit with white markings and a helmet, so the horror only comes out when Flash loses control. Cullen Bunn takes over, moves him to Philadelphia, and then Space Knight sends him into the galaxy as a cosmic hero with the symbiote cleansed and calm.
That last turn is where the run splits readers: it is a genuinely well-made book about a Venom nobody was asking for.

fig.cap: Left: Venom (2011) #1 — Flash Thompson, fifty missions. Right: Space Knight, the same character four years later and a galaxy away.

makers.b: Look at the seams. Moore draws Agent Venom as equipment — panel lines, buckles, a visor with a hard edge — so the moments when the suit goes feral and the mouth opens land as a machine failing rather than as a monster arriving.

sections.h: Cates and Stegman: the run that rebuilt him
body: Donny Cates and Ryan Stegman open in 2018 with Eddie back, broke, hearing things, and then do the single most consequential thing anyone has done with the property: they give the symbiotes a god. Knull existed before light, made the symbiotes as weapons, and was worshipped as a dragon in Viking-age Scandinavia. It is a mythology retrofitted onto a costume, and it is executed with enough conviction that it stuck instantly.

Stegman is the reason. His Venom is not a bodybuilder — he is elongated, wet and asymmetrical, drawn with a scratchy contour and a silhouette that changes shape between panels, so the suit reads as a liquid with opinions. JP Mayer's inks keep it from turning to mud and Frank Martin's colour keeps the black readable, which is a harder job than it sounds on a character who is entirely black.

The other thing the run does is give Eddie a son. Dylan Brock turns the book from a horror comic into a story about inheritance, which is why the ending — Eddie ascending and leaving the suit to the boy — carries weight it has no business carrying.
It runs straight through two events, Absolute Carnage and King in Black, both of which are on this shelf twice: the core minis inside the Cates volume, and the tie-in halves in their own books.

fig.cap: Left: Venom (2018) #1, Stegman. Right: King in Black #1 — three years later, the same idea arrives with a fleet.

makers.b: Compare a Stegman Venom to a Ron Lim one. Lim's has a consistent silhouette from panel to panel; Stegman's does not — the shoulders move, the head lengthens, the tendrils redistribute mass. The inconsistency is deliberate and it is the whole modern look of the character.

Watch how much of the black is actually deep blue and violet. Martin almost never uses true black on the figure, saving it for the background, which is what keeps a black character legible against a dark page. It is the least visible and most necessary craft on the book.

sections.h: Ewing, Ram V, and a war over a father and a son
body: Al Ewing and Ram V follow Cates in 2021 and take the book somewhere nobody expected: a time-travel structure in which Eddie is scattered across his own future, a symbiote hive politics of many Venoms, and a villain called Meridius who is Eddie himself at the end of history. It is the most formally ambitious Venom comic there has been.
None of that run is collected in omnibus. The shelf jumps from 2021 to Venom War in 2024, which is a real hole and Marvel's doing rather than a curation call.

Venom War is where it lands: Eddie and Dylan both have a claim on the symbiote, the symbiote has to choose, and a dozen tie-ins hand a symbiote to everybody else in the building for three issues each. As events go it has an unusually good hook — the fight is a custody dispute — and an unusually large number of tie-ins about Jeff the Land Shark.

fig.cap: Venom War #1, 2024. Iban Coello, and the book is on the shelf a year before it is on a shelf in a shop.

tone.sub: Ten books that disagree completely about whether this is a horror comic, a war comic, a family drama or a joke.

modes.b: The origin volume. McFarlane draws Venom bigger than Spider-Man, standing in his flat, talking to his wife. Nothing later on the shelf is this uncomfortable.

Venomnibus Vol. 1. Foil covers, a million-copy first issue, and eighteen months of three-issue miniseries about a man who lives in a sewer and eats criminals. It is not good and it is completely irreplaceable.
Agent Venom. Remender puts the symbiote on a double amputee who is also the son of an alcoholic, and never explains the metaphor once.
Cates and Stegman. A Venom whose silhouette changes between panels, in colour that is almost never actually black. The modern look of the character starts here.
The Conway Carnage. A serial killer, a cult, an elder god and an FBI agent who cannot sleep — the only book here that reads as horror rather than as a superhero comic wearing horror.
King in Black. Sixty-three issues, symbiote dragons over every city on Earth, and a tie-in for almost everybody Marvel publishes.
Venomnibus Vol. 3. An eighteen-issue ongoing about a symbiote in Antarctic ice that nobody liked in 2003 and a lot of people defend now, ending with Eddie selling the suit at auction.

vsvenom-o1.title: Spider-Man vs. Venom Omnibus
vsvenom-o1.lede: The costume, the man who put it on, and every appearance up to Maximum Carnage — the only book that is on two shelves on this site.

body: The black costume comes back from Secret Wars in May 1984 and for four years the story is entirely about the clothing. The design was bought from a reader, Randy Schueller, for $220 and finished by Mike Zeck; the stretched white spider with no webbing lines is still the best costume redesign Marvel has done.

Amazing Spider-Man #258 is where Reed Richards works out it is alive. #300 is where it finds Eddie Brock, and the thing to notice about that issue is how little fighting is in it — Venom is in Peter's flat, on his ceiling, talking to Mary Jane, and the horror is entirely about knowing where he lives.

Todd McFarlane is drawing Spider-Man at this point and the character is essentially his invention as an image: the excess fabric, the impossible mouth, the tongue. Every Venom since is a response to those pages.

makers.b: The size difference. McFarlane draws Venom a head and a half taller than Spider-Man in almost every shared panel, and stages him above the camera. The threat is blocked before it is written.

fig.cap: Left: #252 — the suit, four years before it has a face. Right: #300.

body: Erik Larsen and then Mark Bagley follow McFarlane and each keeps one thing: Larsen the sheer bulk, Bagley the readability. Bagley's Venom is the one most readers of the decade actually saw, and his Carnage design — the same shape with all the mass taken out — is the smartest piece of visual sequel logic on the shelf.

The book ends on Maximum Carnage, fourteen parts rotating Amazing, Web, Spider-Man and Spectacular month by month, printed here in crossover order rather than by title. It is the story that permanently moves Venom to the hero side of the board.
Note the tail of the volume: Marvel Comics Presents #117–122 is a six-part Venom serial, and the Darkhawk and Spirits of Vengeance issues are here because a 1993 crossover could not be contained.

fig.cap: Where he goes next: Lethal Protector #1, and the next tile.

body: This volume is also on the Spider-Man shelf, and that is deliberate: the issue ids are shared across the site, so Amazing Spider-Man #300 marked read here is marked read there. Both tiles carry the gold "in 2 omnibuses" pill on every issue in it.

It is here because without it the Venom shelf opens in 1993 with a character who already exists, already lives in San Francisco and already has a moral code — which is exactly the wrong place to meet him.

As a reading experience it is uneven by design: it is an appearance chronology, not a run, so it doubles back across Michelinie's two Spider-Man omnibuses and skips whatever Venom is not in. The first hundred pages and the Maximum Carnage stretch are the reasons to have it.

venom-o1.title: Venomnibus Vol. 1
venom-o1.lede: The turn from monster to anti-hero, and the beginning of the strangest publishing plan in 1990s Marvel: eighteen miniseries instead of one ongoing.

body: Six issues, a holographic foil cover, and one of the best-selling comics of the speculation boom. Eddie moves to San Francisco, finds a colony of homeless people living in tunnels under the city, and becomes their protector — on the condition, negotiated with Spider-Man, that he stops eating people Spider-Man would object to.

It is an absurd hairpin turn from #300 and it is executed with total conviction, which is why it worked. The character had been a horror image for five years; he spends this issue rescuing a child from a burning building.

fig.cap: The foil cover, 1993. A million copies, and the moment the character stops being a villain.

body: What follows is the publishing strategy that defines this shelf's middle: three-issue miniseries, one after another, forever. Funeral Pyre with the Punisher. The Madness with the Hulk, which is genuinely deranged and has Kelley Jones art. Nights of Vengeance. Separation Anxiety, where the five symbiote offspring turn up. Carnage Unleashed.
Each one has a #1 to sell, which is the entire logic. Marvel's own explanation at the time was that a monthly Venom would over-expose him; the miniseries did that anyway, at a faster rate.
Ron Lim pencils the bulk of it and the volume is a good place to watch a specific thing: how a clean, well-staged, entirely legible artist can defuse a character built out of ugliness.

makers.b: Look at the mouth. McFarlane's Venom has a jaw that does not close and teeth in the wrong places; Lim's has a consistent, symmetrical grin that resolves the same way every panel. Legible, professional, and not frightening — and that is the decade in one drawing.

body: The recurring criticism is fair and is the one you should expect: the miniseries are repetitive, most run out of story by their third issue, and the volume as a whole is a monument to a sales strategy rather than to a run.

It is also the book most Venom readers actually mean when they talk about Venom. Lethal Protector is the character's defining turn, and if you want to understand what 1993 comics were, this is the single best artefact on the site — foil covers, sewer colonies, guest stars and all.
Read it as an era rather than as a story and it is a pleasure. Read it expecting the Cates volume nine tiles along and it will not survive.

venom-o2.title: Venomnibus Vol. 2
venom-o2.lede: The treadmill runs out. Fourteen more miniseries, one genuinely good one, and the end of the character for a decade.

body: Sinner Takes All is the one worth the volume. The symbiote bonds to Anne Weying, Eddie's ex-wife, and She-Venom is the only idea in the whole mini era with an emotional engine: a woman who has spent years afraid of what her husband became, finding out what it feels like from the inside and liking part of it.

The Hunger is the other one. The symbiote needs phenethylamine, a chemical found in human brains and, awkwardly, in chocolate, and the book has Eddie in an alley eating a fistful of it to keep the thing on his back from taking what it wants. It is both faintly ridiculous and the best horror beat of the era.
On Trial hands Eddie a defence attorney and the attorney is Matt Murdock, which produces the only Venom story that is mostly people talking in a room.

sections.h: The government years, and the stop
body: Tooth and Claw is Wolverine; License to Kill and The Finale put Venom on a government payroll, which is where the 1990s put everybody eventually.

And then it stops. The Finale is titled honestly — there is no Venom ongoing, no further miniseries and effectively no character for the next year. The back of the volume is the odds and ends: the 1995 Planet of the Symbiotes crossover across five Super Specials, an Uncanny Origins retelling, and a Holiday Special.
The gap after this is not on the shelf and does not need to be: there was almost nothing published.

Readers who like the era rate this below Vol. 1 and the reason is structural rather than a matter of taste: Vol. 1 has a genuine turning point in it and this one is the same formula fourteen more times, by which point the market had noticed.
Sinner Takes All is the exception everyone names, and She-Venom has outlived almost everything else here — Anne Weying is still a live character thirty years on.
If you are reading the shelf straight through, this is the volume where the 1990s stop being fun and start being a sales chart. That is worth experiencing once.

venom-o3.title: Venomnibus Vol. 3
venom-o3.lede: The ongoing he was denied in 1993, ten years late — and the only Venom story that ends with a man selling his own symbiote at auction.

body: The volume opens with Venom doing what he had stopped doing in 1993: turning up in Spider-Man's book as the antagonist. Paul Jenkins on Peter Parker: Spider-Man is the best of it — a quieter, sadder Eddie who is losing an argument with the thing on his back.
It is a useful stretch to read after Vol. 2, because it shows the character being carefully de-escalated: no sewer colony, no protector, no foil covers. Just a man and a parasite.

Daniel Way and Francisco Herrera's Venom (2003) is eighteen issues and is the strangest thing on this shelf. A symbiote is recovered from Antarctic ice, and the book withholds almost everything — who is in it, when it is set, whether Eddie is involved — for a long stretch, running on body horror and confusion rather than plot.

Venom Vs. Carnage (2004) is the escalation move one more time and creates Toxin: Carnage's child, bonded against its will to a New York police officer who does not want it. Clayton Crain paints it digitally, and it is the first time the symbiotes look wet rather than drawn.

The end of the volume is the thing to know about. Eddie Brock, dying of cancer, sells the symbiote at auction in Marvel Knights: Spider-Man, and Mac Gargan — the Scorpion — buys it. Everything Venom does for the next eight years, including the Thunderbolts and the Dark Avengers, is somebody else.

fig.cap: Left: the 2003 ongoing. Right: Crain's Venom Vs. Carnage — painted, not inked.

body: The Way run was widely panned on release — the complaints were incoherence, an unlikeable cast and art that readers found hard to follow — and it has since acquired a real defence: that the incoherence is the point, that it is a horror comic rather than a superhero one, and that it is the only Venom book of its decade with an idea.
Both readings are honestly held. It is the volume on this shelf most likely to surprise you in either direction.
Venom Vs. Carnage is the uncontested part: Crain's painted symbiotes are still cited as the moment the visual language modernised. Its cover scan is one of the two low-resolution ones on this shelf.

agent-o1.title: Agent Venomnibus
agent-o1.lede: The symbiote as a controlled substance, worn by a double amputee with fifty missions and a hard clock. The best-written run on the shelf.

body: Rick Remender's premise is the best any Venom writer has had. Flash Thompson — Peter Parker's high-school bully, then an Army sergeant, then a double amputee — is given the symbiote by the US government for fifty missions. It gives him his legs back for the length of each one. Past a time limit it bonds permanently.

Flash's father was an alcoholic and Flash is a drinker, and the book never states the metaphor. It simply gives him something that makes him whole, puts it on a clock, and watches him negotiate with himself about the clock.

The other thing it gets right is the design. Agent Venom is a black tactical suit with white markings and a helmet, and the classic mouth only appears when Flash loses control — so the horror is an event rather than a costume.

makers.b: Watch the mission clocks. Almost every early issue is structured around a countdown, and Remender uses it the way a heist writer uses a vault: the tension is never about whether Flash can win, it is about whether he will take the extra ten minutes.

The hard edges. Moore draws the suit as equipment with seams and panel lines, which gives the artist somewhere to go when it fails: the moment the contour goes soft and organic, you know Flash has lost.

fig.cap: Venom (2011) #1. A war comic with a symbiote in it.

body: Cullen Bunn takes over and moves Flash to Philadelphia as its resident hero, which is the small-scale, street-level half of the run and is generally rated the weaker one.

Then Space Knight (2015) does something nobody predicted: it cleanses the symbiote, makes it a partner rather than a parasite, and sends Flash into the galaxy as a cosmic hero. Ariel Olivetti paints it in bright, open colour — about as far from a horror comic as this character has been.
Minimum Carnage sits in the middle of the volume and crosses into Scarlet Spider; those four issues are also in the Carnage omnibus, one tile along, so they share ids.

fig.cap: Space Knight #1. Same man, cleansed suit, entirely different book.

verdict.standing: Widely held to be the best-written Venom run
body: The Remender stretch is the one readers reach for when arguing that Venom can carry a serious book, and the addiction reading is close to consensus rather than a stretch.

The recurring criticism is that the run changes genre twice — black-ops thriller, then street-level hero book, then cosmic adventure — and that the last turn abandons everything that made the first one work. Readers who love Space Knight and readers who love the Remender issues are frequently not the same people.
It is also, quietly, the most complete run on the shelf: all forty-two issues, every point issue, and Space Knight entire.

carnage-o1.title: Carnage Omnibus
carnage-o1.lede: Cletus Kasady's own shelf — a different character on a Venom shelf, and the volume the user put on deliberately.

body: It opens on Venom Vs. Carnage, which is where Toxin is born, and then runs the whole solo line. Zeb Wells and Clayton Crain's Carnage (2010) brings Cletus back from being torn in half in orbit; Carnage, U.S.A. (2012) is the strongest single story in the volume — Cletus takes an entire Colorado town, everyone in it, at once — and Superior Carnage puts the Wizard in charge of him, which goes as well as expected.

Deadpool vs. Carnage and AXIS: Carnage are the tonal outliers: the first is a comedy, the second inverts him into a hero for three issues. Both are symptoms of the same problem — a character with one note, being played by people looking for a second.

The last sixteen issues are the reason to own this. Gerry Conway — who wrote the death of Gwen Stacy in 1973 — comes back and writes Carnage as a straight horror serial: an FBI task force chasing Cletus into a cave system, a cult, the Darkhold, and the elder god Chthon.

Mike Perkins draws it in heavy blacks with almost no superhero staging, and the book keeps its cast small and its body count personal. It is the only thing on this shelf that reads as horror rather than as a superhero comic wearing horror.
John Jameson and Eddie Brock are both in the task force, which is how a Carnage volume earns a place on a Venom shelf.

fig.cap: Carnage (2015) #1, Conway and Perkins. Almost nobody read it.

makers.b: Count the panels per page. Perkins runs six and seven where a superhero book runs four, and shoots most of them tight on faces in torchlight. The claustrophobia is a layout decision before it is a colour one.

body: The Conway/Perkins run is the volume's real recommendation and is routinely described as the best Carnage material there is and the least read. The middle stretch — Superior Carnage, AXIS, the Deadpool crossover — is where the sequel problem shows: readers generally find the character works as a threat and not as a lead.

It is on this shelf because the user put it there. By the reasoning that keeps She-Hulk off the Hulk shelf and Laura Kinney off Wolverine's, Cletus is a different character — roughly ten of its fifty-two issues are Venom or Spider-Man titles.

The counter-argument, and the reason it earns its place: Absolute Carnage two tiles along is unreadable as anything but a sequel to this, and Toxin, Scream and the whole symbiote family come out of it.

cates-o1.title: Venomnibus by Cates & Stegman
cates-o1.lede: The run that gave the symbiotes a god, gave Eddie a son, and reset what the character looks like. The centre of the shelf.

body: Donny Cates and Ryan Stegman open with Eddie broke, hallucinating and living badly, and by the third issue have introduced a god who predates light. Knull made the symbiotes as weapons, was worshipped in Viking-age Scandinavia as a dragon, and has been imprisoned inside a planet made of the things ever since.

It is a retrofit of enormous scale onto a character who was a costume in 1984, and the reason it stuck rather than being quietly dropped is that it explains something that had always been unexplained: why a costume has teeth.

The first arc, Rex, is a Vietnam war story with a symbiote in it — Web of Venom: Ve'Nam is printed alongside it here — and it establishes the run's actual register, which is closer to a horror-war comic than to a superhero book.

makers.b: The silhouette does not hold. Track Venom across three consecutive panels and his shoulders, head length and mass all change. Every artist before Stegman treated the suit as a costume with a constant shape; he treats it as a volume of liquid, and that is why his Venom looks alive and everyone else's looks dressed.

Look for actual black on the figure — there is almost none. Martin renders the suit in deep blues and violets and saves true black for the background, which is the only reason a black character stays readable on a dark page.

fig.cap: Left: #1. Right: #4 — by here the book has a god in it and the shape of the character has already changed.

body: The second half turns the book into a story about inheritance. Dylan Brock is Eddie's son, and the run's real subject becomes whether a man made of appetite can hand anything to a child without ruining it.

Both of Cates's events run straight through here: Absolute Carnage (2019) and King in Black (2020). This volume prints their core minis only — the tie-in halves are the next two tiles, which is why the shelf carries all three.

It ends with Eddie ascending: he takes Knull's place, becomes the god of the symbiotes, and leaves the suit to his son. It is an enormous ending for a character who started as a costume, and the run earns most of it.

fig.cap: King in Black #1 — the payoff of a reveal made three years earlier.

body: This is the run people mean now when they say Venom, and the consensus on it is unusually strong: the best-regarded Venom material there has been, and the one that made the character a load-bearing part of the Marvel universe rather than a Spider-Man villain with good merchandise.

The recurring criticism is specific and worth knowing: Cates retcons constantly, and readers who came in through the 1990s books find that the history is rewritten under them — the symbiote's origin, Eddie's history, the nature of the bond. The other complaint is that the back half runs on event scheduling rather than on the story, and that King in Black's ending arrives faster than it earns.
Neither objection is usually offered as a reason not to read it. Start the shelf here if you are only reading one book.

abscarn-o1.title: Absolute Carnage Omnibus
abscarn-o1.lede: The tie-in half of the 2019 event — fourteen miniseries and one-shots around a core the previous tile already prints.

sections.h: A premise built to reach everywhere
body: Cletus comes back wanting the codex — a residue left in the spine of everyone who has ever worn a symbiote — which is a plot device engineered to give every character in the building a reason to be in the story. Roughly a third of the Marvel line has worn one at some point.

The core five issues are here and are also in the Cates volume, so those ids are shared. What this book adds is the fourteen tie-ins: vs. Deadpool, Miles Morales, Scream, Lethal Protectors, Immortal Hulk, Captain Marvel, Weapon Plus, Separation Anxiety.
Scream is the one to look for. Andi Benton and the Scream symbiote get three issues of genuine character work in the middle of an event, which is more than the format usually allows.
The tail of the volume is the lead-in: single issues from Amazing Spider-Man, Fantastic Four, Immortal Hulk, Avengers, Invaders and Black Cat where Carnage picks his victims off one at a time.

fig.cap: Left: Absolute Carnage #1. Right: Scream — the tie-in worth the volume.

verdict.standing: Divisive — as event tie-in collections are
body: The core mini is generally well received: it is a deliberate Maximum Carnage homage done thirty years later with a better artist, and readers who grew up on the 1993 version rate it highly.

The tie-ins are the argument. The recurring criticism of this book specifically is that a large number of them exist to hand a symbiote to a character for one issue, and that reading fourteen of them consecutively is a different and much worse experience than reading them monthly around the core.
The honest recommendation: this is a companion volume, not a starting point. Read the Cates tile first and come here for Scream, Lethal Protectors and the lead-in issues.

kib-o1.title: King in Black Omnibus
kib-o1.lede: Sixty-three issues — the widest book on the shelf, and the payoff of a reveal made three years earlier.

body: Knull arrives, blacks out the sun over Earth, and drops symbiote dragons on every city at once. As a piece of staging it is the most striking thing Marvel has done with the property: an entire planet in the dark, with everyone's costume being rewritten from underneath.

The core five are also in the Cates volume. What this book adds is the whole line: Namor, S.W.O.R.D., Black Cat, Savage Avengers, Thunderbolts, Return of the Valkyries, Planet of the Symbiotes, Gwenom vs. Carnage and about twenty one-shots.
Namor is the standout — five issues of Atlantean prehistory that have almost nothing to do with the event and are better than most of it. Return of the Valkyries is the other one people name.

fig.cap: King in Black #1. The sun is off for the whole book.

body: The consensus on the core is that it looks magnificent and resolves too quickly: Stegman's dragons and blacked-out cities are among the best spectacle Marvel has printed, and the ending — which turns on a very large power-up arriving late — is the most common complaint about the whole Cates era.
The tie-ins split hard. Several are genuinely good books that happen to have an event stapled to them; a larger number are one-shots in which a hero fights a symbiote dragon for twenty pages.
It is on the shelf because the Cates volume prints the core and nothing else, so without this the tie-in half of a story that shelf spends three years building to is simply absent.

venomwar-o1.title: Venom War Omnibus
venomwar-o1.lede: Ships December 2026. A father and a son with one symbiote between them — and the book that opens three years after the run in front of it stopped being collected.

body: Not yet published. It is on the shelf ahead of its December 2026 date because its contents, its deep links and its jacket are all real, which is the bar a tile has to clear here.

Al Ewing and Iban Coello's hook is better than an event usually gets: Eddie Brock and Dylan Brock both have a legitimate claim on the symbiote, the symbiote has to choose between them, and neither of them is wrong. It is a custody dispute fought by two people who can lift a bus.

Around it, the standard modern event architecture: eleven tie-in miniseries handing a symbiote to Spider-Man, Wolverine, Deadpool, Daredevil, the Fantastic Four, Black Widow — and, inevitably, Venom War: It's Jeff, in which the Land Shark gets one.

Note where the volume starts: Venom (2021) #35. Al Ewing and Ram V's #1–34 in front of it — the time-travel run with Meridius and the many Venoms, and the best-reviewed Venom book since Cates — has no omnibus at all, which is the largest hole on this shelf.

verdict.standing: Not yet shipped — no verdict to report
body: The comics themselves ran through 2024 and were received as a solidly built event with an unusually strong central relationship and a very large number of tie-ins; the recurring criticism is the one every modern event gets, which is that the tie-in count outruns the story.
What cannot be reported is a verdict on the book, because it does not exist yet. The contents here are Marvel's own solicited collecting line, which matches the wiki's issue list exactly.

Its jacket is Iban Coello's, taken from the retailer's flat cover image rather than from the Marvel Database, which has no scan for an unshipped book. It is the lowest-resolution tile on the shelf and should be refetched once the book is out.
